title: Infra GPU fleet capacity + Cloud Accounts, Networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD — Guidance (2026)
author: Maya Thompson
summary: Consolidated guidance for operating Redwood's GPU fleet: capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module best practices, CI/CD for infra modules and images, and operator runbooks for day-2 operations and emergency procedures.
body:
Purpose
This doc consolidates the most important operational guidance for the GPU fleet and supporting infra components used by Redwood inference: capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module design and lifecycle, CI/CD pipelines for module releases and AMI/container builds, capacity scaling, and runbook procedures for routine and emergency operations. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners.

Scope
- Applies to hosted and dedicated GPU pools (public cloud regions) and Private deployment networking reference architectures.
- Covers Terraform modules, state management, CI/CD for module releases and AMI/container builds, capacity scaling, and troubleshooting runbooks.
- Does not replace customer-specific on-prem packaging docs; see eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures for on-prem specifics.

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-gpu-capacity team (oncall: infra-gpu-sre@redwood.internal)
- Module ownership: each Terraform module includes an OWNERS file; primary reviewers listed in module README.
- Escalation: infra oncall -> infra-sre lead (Ethan Cole) -> Platform VP (Olivia Grant)

High-level architecture
- GPU pools are provisioned per region and per capacity tier (spot/burst, reserved/dedicated). Key services:
  - capacity-orchestrator (internal service) — manages logical pools and autoscaling policies.
  - gpu-node-manager — instance lifecycle (drain, cordon, node labels).
  - routing-layer (smart-routing) — routes inference traffic by latency/cost policy.
- State is stored in remote Terraform backends (S3 with DynamoDB locks for AWS; GCS + Cloud Locking pattern for GCP).

Capacity planning and SLOs
- Goal SLOs for inference-facing services:
  - 99.9% request success rate (5xx rate <0.1%)
  - P50 latency target per model family as listed in model-catalog (e.g., p50 <= 120ms for small models; p50 <= 600ms for 13B models on dedicated pools)
- Capacity metrics to monitor (minimum set):
  - available_gpu_count (by region, instance_type, quantization_profile)
  - avg_queue_time_ms and queue_length (per pool)
  - pod_startup_time_ms / instance_boot_time_ms
  - evictions/spot-termination-rate and preemption_count
- Target buffer policy: maintain a 15% headroom relative to committed throughput for dedicated pools; for hosted pools keep average queue_length < 5 requests per 1k capacity units during peak 95th percentile windows.

Capacity scaling playbook (routine)
1. Review demand trends on dashboards (dashboards/gpu-capacity-ops) for the last 7/30/90 days.
2. If sustained utilization > 80% for 3 consecutive days in a region for a specific instance type, open RFC and schedule a capacity bump:
   - Create change: terraform plan for module aws_gpu_pool with new desired_count (PR templates in infra-modules/gpu/README).
   - Run pre-deploy Canary in low-risk AZ (20% of change). Monitor for 60 minutes.
   - Roll forward remaining AZs with automated pipeline.
3. For sudden spikes: trigger temporary burst pools (spot with autoscaling); coordinate with product on expected traffic windows.

Emergency capacity request (fast path)
- Criteria: observed 5xx > 0.5% and P95 latency > 2x target, with clear correlation to capacity saturation.
- Steps:
  1) Page infra-gpu oncall (pager duty: infra-gpu).
  2) Scale up dedicated pool using capacity-orchestrator quickscale endpoint: POST /v1/pools/{pool}/quickscale with body {"delta_instances": N, "reason": "emergency"}. (This endpoint requires token from vault path secret/tools/quickscale.)
  3) If quickscale fails or exceeds quota, failover traffic to cheaper model-variants or fallback region using routing-layer (runbook command: rlayer switch --policy fallback-to-variant).
  4) Post-incident, open a postmortem and convert fixes to infra changes (TF PR or capacity-plan RFC).

Cloud accounts and networking patterns
- Account structure:
  - prod-{region} (primary prod workloads)
  - infra-{region} (shared infra services: load balancers, NAT, central logging)
  - tools and sandbox accounts for CI/CD and long-running test harnesses
- VPC design guidance:
  - Dedicated GPU pools run in customer VPCs (private deployments) or Redwood-managed VPCs for hosted. Use /20 CIDR for cluster subnets; reserve /24 per AZ for expansion.
  - Use separate subnets for control-plane, worker-gpu, and mgmt (bastion/NAT).
  - Enforce egress via central NAT gateway where possible; prefer VPC endpoints for object storage access to keep metadata off the public internet.
- Routing & security:
  - Use AWS Security Groups with least-privilege: allow only kubelet, SSH from management subnets, and service mesh ports.
  - Enforce network ACLs for cross-account peering boundaries; require approval via change control for any open ingress rule > /32.

Terraform / IaC module standards
- Module layout (required files): README.md, variables.tf, outputs.tf, main.tf, versions.tf, tests/ (unit & integration), OWNERS.
- Naming: module names use kebab-case and short names: infra/gpu-pool, infra/vpc, infra/s3-backend.
- State management: use remote state buckets with encryption-at-rest and state locking (DynamoDB for AWS). Cross-account access via IAM role assumption (role name: terra-state-access).
- Versioning and releases: semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Release flow:
  1) Branch -> PR with CHANGELOG entry -> CI runs unit tests + terratest integration against a dedicated test account.
  2) After merging, create a git tag vX.Y.Z and push release; the release CI publishes module artifact to the internal module registry.
- Testing: every module must have:
  - unit: terraform validate + tflint + checkov
  - integration: terratest run in isolated test account (CI job: ci/infra/integration)
- Best practices: avoid embedding secrets; reference secrets via vault data sources. Keep small modules and compose with higher-level stacks.

CI/CD and build pipelines
- Pipelines hosted in CircleCI / GitHub Actions hybrid (see infra-ci pipeline docs). Key pipelines:
  - ci/infra/lint-and-test: runs terraform fmt, tflint, checkov, terraform validate.
  - ci/infra/integration: runs terratest against dedicated test accounts (parallel regions when applicable).
  - ci/infra/release: on tag push, publishes module package to internal registry and updates module versions in parent repo via automated PRs.
- Build artifacts: GPU node images are built by image-builder pipeline (packer -> artifact store). Images are signed and stored in image registry with tags: redwood/gpu-node:<image_version>-<sha>.
- Rollouts: use canary pipeline that deploys new module/image to 1 AZ/10% of capacity, runs smoke tests for 30-60 minutes, then progressive rollout to remaining AZs. Failure auto-rolls back to previous artifact.

Runbooks and common operational procedures
- Node drain for failed GPU nodes:
  1) awscli: aws ec2 create-tags --resources <instance-id> --tags Key=maintenance,Value=true
  2) kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  3) Verify pod rescheduling and workload health (kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep Pending)
- Replace failed instance:
  - For AWS: terraform apply will replace AutoscalingGroup desired_capacity; for manual, use aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids <id> then monitor autoscaling activity.
- Routine maintenance window (weekly low-traffic window):
  - Announce 48h in advance; run canary upgrades first; ensure 2x buffer in dedicated pools before rolling changes.

Debugging checklist (quick)
- If queue_length rising: check available_gpu_count and pod_startup_time_ms. Long boot times often point to subnet NAT throughput or AMI/kernel issues.
- If evictions spike: check spot-termination-rate and switch workloads to reserved nodes; apply eviction-tolerant taints where appropriate.
- If Terraform apply fails with lock error: verify DynamoDB table for locks and that the CI role can assume terra-state-access role.

Postmortem and change process
- Any incident with customer impact requires a postmortem within 72 hours. Postmortem must include timeline, root cause, mitigation, and follow-ups assigned to owners. Follow-ups that require infra changes should open a TF PR with the intended fix and a rollout plan.

Appendix: common commands and snippets
- Example remote backend (AWS):
  terraform {
    backend "s3" {
      bucket = "redwood-terraform-state-prod"
      key    = "infra/gpu-pool/terraform.tfstate"
      region = "us-west-2"
      dynamodb_table = "redwood-terraform-locks"
      encrypt = true
    }
  }

- Quickscale curl example (internal; requires vault token):
  curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/v1/pools/gpu-us-west-2-13b/quickscale \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $QUICKSCALE_TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"delta_instances": 10, "reason": "emergency traffic spike"}'
